Meropenem is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that can be found in both interstitial fluid (IF) and plasma concentrations. However, the current evidence does not suggest that these two concentrations are equivalent in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT).

In fact, studies have shown that meropenem IF concentrations are significantly lower than plasma concentrations, even when administered at appropriate doses for infections caused by intermediate-susceptible pathogens. This is because meropenem can be distributed into the interstitial space more easily due to its lipophilic nature.

The use of central venous pressure (CVP) as a predictor of fluid responsiveness has been shown not to be reliable in critically ill patients receiving CRRT. Other factors, such as cardiac output and intravascular volume status, are more closely related to fluid management than CVP.

Therefore, based on the available evidence, it is recommended that clinicians do not rely solely on CVP to guide fluid therapy in critically ill patients receiving CRRT. Instead, they should use a combination of clinical assessments, laboratory tests, and hemodynamic monitoring to determine adequate fluid status and optimal fluid resuscitation strategies.

It's worth noting that further research may be needed to fully understand the relationship between meropenem IF concentrations and plasma concentrations, as well as the effects of CRRT on fluid management in critically ill patients.
